newsitem.title: USA: Industry, critics, react to tobacco ruling.
newsitem.headline: Industry, critics, react to tobacco ruling.

text.p: Cigarette makers said Friday that they would contest part of a ruling by a federal judge in North Carolina that the Food and Drug Administration has authority to regulate sales and labeling of cigarettes.
Meanwhile, while anti-smoking groups hailed the ruling.

"As far as I can tell it is a spectacular ruling for the public health and for the FDA," said Professor Richard Daynard of the Tobacco Products Liability Project, a public health lobbying group at Northeastern University in Boston, referring to the Food and Drug Administration.

"You have a judge in the heart of tobacco country ruling that nicotine is a drug and that cigarettes and smokeless tobacco are drug delivery devices," Daynard said by telephone after reading news accounts of the ruling.

U.S. District Court Judge William Osteen ruled in North Carolina, one of the leading tobacco-producing states, that the FDA can regulate sales and labeling on cigarettes but cannot regulate advertising of tobacco products.
The tobacco industry had challenged as unconstitutional new curbs on advertising and marketing of cigarettes imposed by federal regulators.
The cigarette companies said they would contest facts asserted by the government that were the basis for Osteen's ruling.
"The court noted that the industry can contest those factual assertions as the case proceeds -- and we will," the tobacco companies said in a joint statement.
Osteen heard arguments in February that the FDA had overstepped its authority and was violating U.S. free-speech guarantees with its new rules limiting the sale and advertising of cigarettes.
The ruling comes as cigarette makers are under growing pressure to settle lawsuits seeking billions of dollars for smoking-related illness.
Daynard of the Tobacco Products Liablity Project said the ruling would hurt the industry's position in those cases, and negotiations aimed at settling them.
"This tremendously weakens the industry's hand in negotiations as well as in the current and impending lawsuits, if they proceed," he said.
Anti-smoking advocates in Congress also hailed the ruling.
The Clinton administration, while praising most of the ruling, said it would appeal the part of the ruling stating the FDA cannot regulate cigarette advertising and promotion.
Tobacco stocks fell after the ruling, which traders said was mixed but more negative for cigarette makers.

Philip Morris, the world's largest tobacco company whose brands include Marlboro, fell $2.25 to $39.375, RJR Nabisco Holdings lost $1.75 to $29.875 and Loews Corp., which owns Lorillard, dropped $1.875 to $89.75, all on the New York Stock Exchange.
